question: Can benchmark correlations be compressed into a few latent skills whose shared parameter/token response curves forecast larger models across families after observing only one small model from a new family?

key_findings.claim: Sloth couples a low-rank benchmark factor model to family-adjusted parameter/token scaling.
key_findings.evidence: Benchmark logits equal a loading matrix times d latent skills plus biases. Each skill is a translog function of log parameters, log training tokens, and their interaction; slopes are shared across families while a per-family intercept represents conversion efficiency. Optional monotone neural link functions map logits to scores.

key_findings.claim: Cross-family leaderboard prediction is competitive when one or two members of the held-out family are observed.
key_findings.evidence: Leave-family-out experiments over 30 families and 12 Open LLM Leaderboard v1/v2 benchmarks reveal similar or lower mean absolute error than FLOPs, PCA-plus-FLOPs, and full-rank size/tokens variants. Results are reported across individual families and alternative error metrics, though the main plots do not provide uncertainty intervals.

key_findings.claim: The named skills are rotated statistical factors, not uniquely identified cognitive mechanisms.
key_findings.evidence: The basic model is identifiable only up to latent transformations; the authors whiten and use Geomin rotation, then subjectively name dimensions from benchmark loadings. With d=3 they call factors reasoning, knowledge, and instruction following, but the instruction-following interpretation does not persist at d=4.

key_findings.claim: Sloth supports downstream and test-time-compute forecasts, but evidence consists of a few retrospective held-out models.
key_findings.evidence: Predicted skills feed logistic models for Llama-3-70B HumanEval, EQ-Bench, and AgentBench and item-response models for MATH pass@k on three held-out family members. The appendix reports comparable out-of-sample error to observational scaling on the two showcased downstream tasks; no prospective expensive model training validates investment decisions.

key_findings.claim: Compute-optimal skill allocations are model extrapolations constrained to historical support, not experimentally established optima.
key_findings.evidence: The paper analytically optimizes each fitted translog skill at fixed 6st compute and clips parameter/token choices to training-data quantiles. No models are trained at the recommended allocations, and different latent rotations can change which factor is optimized.

method.core_idea: Borrow statistical strength across benchmarks and model families by treating observed scores as nonlinear measurements of a few compute-scaled latent factors.
method.mechanism: Fit robust Huber loss to leaderboard scores using low-rank loadings, family intercepts, shared translog slopes, benchmark lower asymptotes, and fixed or learned monotone links; rotate the latent space for interpretation and extrapolate skills to larger size/token pairs.
assumptions: A low-dimensional factor space explains benchmark score covariance.
Families share skill scaling slopes and differ mainly by intercept efficiency.
Reported parameter and training-token counts are comparable and accurate.
Benchmark score/link behavior remains stable outside the observed size range.
At least one representative model from the target family is usually available.

techniques.role: Reduces per-benchmark scaling parameters through shared latent dimensions.
Absorbs architecture, data, and post-training differences using one observed family member.
Separates parameter and token effects and allows their interaction.
Fits benchmark-specific saturation curves while enforcing score monotonicity.
Whitenes and rotates skills to obtain sparse, human-labeled loadings.

evaluations.setting: Open LLM Leaderboard v1/v2: 30 base families, 53 when base/instruct are separated, and 12 benchmarks.
evaluations.metric: Leave-family-out mean absolute error when one smallest target-family model is observed.
evaluations.result: Sloth is often the lowest-error method and is similar to or better than a full-rank size-and-tokens model.
evaluations.baseline: Shared/family-intercept FLOPs laws, PCA+FLOPs, and no-low-rank size/tokens scaling.

evaluations.metric: Held-out HumanEval and EQ-Bench score prediction.
evaluations.result: Predicted latent skills yield visually close held-out scores; comparative appendix results are similar to observational scaling out of sample.

evaluations.setting: MATH question-level predictions for held-out large Llama 3, Gemma, and Pythia models.
evaluations.metric: Pass@k curve as sampling compute increases.
evaluations.result: Skill-conditioned item-response predictions track the displayed empirical test-time curves.
evaluations.baseline: Observed pass@k and direct family scaling alternatives.

limitations: Author-stated: prediction usually needs at least one member of the target family.
Author-stated: learned neural links can interpolate well without any out-of-support extrapolation guarantee.
Author-stated: identifiability is understood only for the simpler fixed-link/lower-asymptote model.
Reviewer inference: leaderboard contamination, evaluation noise, estimated token counts, and correlated model lineages can masquerade as stable skills.
Reviewer inference: the paper reports no conventional uncertainty intervals and no genuinely prospective training-run validation.
failure_modes: A new family changes scaling slopes rather than only intercept efficiency.
Benchmark saturation or a capability discontinuity occurs beyond observed scales.
A latent rotation produces an appealing name that is unstable across d, benchmark set, or leaderboard version.
One small family model is unrepresentative because post-training/data quality changes at larger sizes.
Public benchmark scores are contaminated or use inconsistent harness versions.
reusable_insights: Multi-output scaling can reduce variance by modeling benchmark covariance explicitly.
Family adaptation should separate what one anchor model identifies from what cross-family data assumes.
Latent-factor names need stability analyses across rotations, dimensions, and benchmark subsets.
Forecasting should output calibrated intervals and be validated prospectively before guiding expensive runs.
open_questions: Do shared skill slopes hold for families designed after the training corpus and evaluation suite?
Can hierarchical Bayesian Sloth provide calibrated extrapolation intervals and lineage dependence?
Which skills remain stable after contamination-resistant or newly created benchmarks replace leaderboard tasks?
Do recommended compute allocations win in actual matched-FLOP training experiments?

competitive_landscape.title: Observational Scaling Laws and the Predictability of Language Model Performance
competitive_landscape.difference: Ruan et al. also infer low-dimensional capabilities and family compute efficiency from public models; Sloth separates parameters/tokens, regularizes scores jointly through factor loadings, and targets prediction before the large family member exists.

competitive_landscape.title: How predictable is language model benchmark performance?
competitive_landscape.difference: Owen fits aggregate/task compute laws across architectures and documents high task-level error; Sloth conditions on family anchors and benchmark covariance through latent skills.

competitive_landscape.title: Language models scale reliably with over-training and on downstream tasks
competitive_landscape.difference: Gadre et al. train a controlled 104-model grid and map validation loss to aggregate downstream error; Sloth uses heterogeneous public leaderboard observations to avoid new training runs.

competitive_landscape.title: Scaling Laws for Downstream Task Performance of Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Isik et al. model downstream transfer under controlled pretraining/finetuning data alignment; Sloth models many heterogeneous benchmarks and families via shared latent factors.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Low-dimensional skills yield accurate, interpretable, parameter-efficient scaling laws across families and enable downstream/test-time/compute-optimal prediction.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Leave-family-out leaderboard comparisons, factor loadings, three application studies, and identifiability results for a basic variant support this within the assembled data.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The parameter/token factorization and one-anchor-family prediction are useful extensions of observational scaling, but the latent skills are exploratory statistics and prospective extrapolation risk remains largely unmeasured.

reviewer_notes: Read all 46 pages, including identifiability, rotation, per-family errors, downstream comparisons, and checklist caveats. Closest primary arXiv scaling-law records were checked on 2026-08-23.
